# Heuristic & Mental Models

<!-- Generated by packages/rules/generate.mjs from data/laws/*.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

11 card(s). Check the code in front of you against each one that applies.

## HMM-01 — Jakob's Law

- **Axiom:** Users spend most time on other interfaces, expecting yours to function identically.
- **Apply when:** Users hesitate, hunt for navigation, or misuse controls because the layout diverges from conventions they know from other products.
- **Check:**
  - Anchor the logo top-left, global navigation top or left, and account controls top-right.
  - Keep checkout steps in the expected billing, shipping, and payment order.
  - Preserve standard keyboard shortcuts and browser history behavior; never hijack them.
- **Instead of:** A web app rebinds the browser back button to internal tab switching and buries global search in the footer.
- **Do:** Call history.pushState or replaceState for back entries; keep search in a persistent header input focused with /, a key the page receives before the browser's quick-find default, not Cmd/Ctrl+K, which the browser reserves as a command.
- **Source:** Jakob Nielsen (2000), *Designing Web Usability: The Practice of Simplicity*.

## HMM-02 — Mental Model Theory

- **Axiom:** People act on a simplified internal model of a system, not the system itself.
- **Apply when:** Users invent their own account of how a feature works, then blame the interface when that account predicts the wrong result.
- **Check:**
  - Name folders, tags, and documents after the objects users already handle in their work.
  - Update the status view from the same event that performed the action, not from a poll.
  - Keep storage terms such as rows, records, and foreign keys out of user-facing labels.
  - Ask users to predict what an action will do before they use it, and record each wrong prediction. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** An email client labels a delete action with a database operation, so saving a draft looks like destroying a record.
- **Do:** Delete moves the message to a Trash folder and states that it stays recoverable for 30 days before purging.
- **Source:** Kenneth Craik (1943), *The Nature of Explanation*.

## HMM-03 — Conceptual Integrity

- **Axiom:** Every module should express the same set of design ideas in the same way.
- **Apply when:** Two screens in one product use different labels, layouts, or gestures for the same job, so each has to be learned from scratch.
- **Check:**
  - Open the same kind of record the same way everywhere: one dialog, one drawer, or one page.
  - Give one permission level one verb across the product; grep the interface strings for synonyms.
  - Render page headers from one component so type, spacing, and breadcrumbs cannot drift apart.
- **Instead of:** A dashboard creates a project in a modal, a task on a new page, and a client in a drawer.
- **Do:** All record creation opens the same slide-over sheet, with the same button order and unsaved-changes guard.
- **Source:** Frederick P. Brooks Jr. (1975), *The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering*.

## HMM-04 — Aesthetic-Usability Effect

- **Axiom:** Polished interfaces are judged more usable than plain ones that do the same work.
- **Apply when:** A restyle changes only color, type, and spacing; testers still rate the product easier to use and stop noticing its flaws.
- **Check:**
  - Derive every margin, padding, and gap from one 4 or 8 pixel scale; no arbitrary values.
  - Align text baselines and control edges to shared guides, and check the page at 100 percent zoom.
  - Draw border radii, shadow levels, and neutral colors from one token file.
  - Test perceived usability separately from task completion; a high aesthetic score is not task success. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** An analytics product ships default browser buttons, misaligned table columns, and unstyled alert text.
- **Do:** It uses tabular figures, one radius scale, and a neutral ramp, with spacing tokens shared across the product.
- **Source:** Masaaki Kurosu & Kaori Kashimura (1995), *Apparent usability vs. inherent usability*.

## HMM-05 — Principle of Least Astonishment (POLA)

- **Axiom:** A control should do what its appearance and label lead people to expect.
- **Apply when:** A familiar control does something unexpected: Save clears the form, a filter reloads the page.
- **Check:**
  - Keep a control's label and function stable across hover, focus, and click; never swap its action.
  - Preserve typed values when server validation fails and mark the failing fields beside them.
  - Give destructive actions an undo window or a confirmation that names the object being removed.
  - Record where users hesitate or backtrack after an action, and treat each as a violated expectation. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** Pressing Save Draft clears every field and shows no confirmation, so the draft exists in local storage or nowhere.
- **Do:** Save Draft shows a saved-at timestamp, keeps the fields filled, and syncs in the background.
- **Source:** M. F. Cowlishaw (1984), *The design of the REXX language*.

## HMM-06 — Postel's Law (Robustness Principle)

- **Axiom:** Accept input in the forms people send; emit output in one strict form.
- **Apply when:** Valid input is rejected over formatting, or downstream services each get a different shape.
- **Check:**
  - Strip spaces, hyphens, and parentheses from phone and card fields before validating them.
  - Parse dates against an explicit list of accepted formats and show those forms beside the field.
  - Emit one canonical format from the API boundary and validate the payload against a schema.
- **Instead of:** Checkout rejects a card number because the user typed spaces between the digit groups, and the error says invalid characters.
- **Do:** The field accepts any delimiter, removes non-digits, and displays the number in grouped blocks as it is typed.
- **Source:** Jon Postel (1980), *DoD standard Transmission Control Protocol*.

## HMM-07 — Occam's Razor (Principle of Parsimony)

- **Axiom:** Prefer the design that explains everything with the fewest added assumptions.
- **Apply when:** Options and edge-case branches pile up until nobody can describe the main path.
- **Check:**
  - Delete gradients, dividers, and wrapper elements that carry no content and no state.
  - Render one primary action on a transactional screen and demote the rest below it.
  - Merge Filter, Sort, and Search into one query bar when they act on the same collection.
  - Time first-time users on the main task before and after a simplification, not just their opinion of it. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** An editor shows 45 toolbar buttons for rare typographic cases, so new writers cannot find bold or undo.
- **Do:** A bare canvas appears first, with a contextual toolbar only while text is selected.
- **Source:** John Maeda (2006), *The Laws of Simplicity*.

## HMM-08 — Conway's Law

- **Axiom:** A system's structure ends up copying the communication structure of the teams that built it.
- **Apply when:** Two teams own half a flow each, and the product asks users to cross a seam no user would draw.
- **Check:**
  - Organise menus by the user's jobs, not by the departments that own the backend services.
  - Share one set of design tokens across services so separately built screens look related.
  - Merge settings the back end splits across services behind one account screen.
  - Before a reorganisation ships, map its team boundaries onto the screens users must cross. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** A telecom portal sends customers to three subdomains with different themes to manage phone, broadband, and billing.
- **Do:** One identity and one design shell put all three offerings in a single services dashboard.
- **Source:** Melvin E. Conway (1968), *How Do Committees Invent?*

## HMM-09 — Gulf of Execution and Gulf of Evaluation

- **Axiom:** Keep intent, action, and visible result close enough that people never have to guess.
- **Apply when:** A button gives no sign it worked, so people click again and create duplicate orders.
- **Check:**
  - Mark clickable elements with a signifier users can see before they hover or click.
  - Change the control and show a status line as soon as an action is accepted.
  - State in the error message what happened, which object it concerned, and the next step.
  - Ask users to describe what the system did after each action; treat a wrong answer as a gulf. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** Clicking Process leaves the cursor unchanged and shows nothing, so the operator clicks three times and files three orders.
- **Do:** The button disables itself, shows a spinner, and relabels to Processing until the result appears.
- **Source:** Donald A. Norman (1986), *Cognitive Engineering*.

## HMM-10 — Affordance Theory

- **Axiom:** An object's properties suggest what can be done with it, before any label says so.
- **Apply when:** A control that works looks exactly like the text around it, so nobody tries it.
- **Check:**
  - Give every control a fill, border, or weight the surrounding text does not have.
  - Keep links underlined or coloured at rest; hover styling alone is not a signifier.
  - Draw a grip on anything draggable, and make the whole surface respond to the drag.
  - Watch first-time users try to click; every dead click marks an affordance that was not visible. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** Call-to-action buttons are set as plain text with no border, fill, or underline, identical to body copy.
- **Do:** Controls sit in filled rounded containers that contrast with the surface and lift on hover.
- **Source:** James J. Gibson (1977), *The Theory of Affordances*.

## HMM-11 — Feedback Principle (Cybernetic Loop)

- **Axiom:** People can steer only what reports back what their last action did.
- **Apply when:** A long upload shows nothing until it finishes, so people reload and start it again.
- **Check:**
  - Show a state change on every control as soon as it is pressed, not when the request returns.
  - Keep a progress indicator for any operation that outlasts a second or two.
  - Report the outcome of a save where the user is looking, not only in a toast that fades.
  - Measure how long the interface takes to acknowledge an action, and treat silence as a defect. _(research: an experiment or a recorded run; not checkable from code)_
- **Instead of:** A file drop zone looks the same while a file is dragged over it, so the user cannot tell whether a drop will be accepted.
- **Do:** The zone outlines itself, tints its surface, and shows Drop files to upload while a file is over it.
- **Source:** Norbert Wiener (1948), *Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine*.
